name: The Holm Oak of St David's Cathedral

location.address: St David's Cathedral, corner of Murray and Macquarie Streets, Hobart

access: Free, public street corner outside the cathedral, always visible
transport: Central Hobart CBD, walkable from anywhere in the city centre
verify_notes: City of Hobart Significant Tree Register ref M9 (23 Murray Street, St Davids Cathedral): Category 1 (outstanding aesthetic significance) and Category 2 (outstanding dimensions). Stands at what is described (Our City Canopy, National Trust) as 'the finest colonial intersection in Australia'. Speculated, not confirmed, to have grown from an acorn or sapling collected at Gallipoli after 1915 as a WWI commemorative planting; no documentary proof, age is an inference from this story plus size, so treat as unconfirmed. National Trust (trusttrees.org.au) measured it 30 March 2014: 16m tall, 2m girth, condition 'Good'. Our City Canopy (article dated 18 Sept 2023, 'Safeguarding the Holm Oak') reports the tree 'has been in decline for some years' despite maintenance efforts, and documents an active propagation programme: one offspring germinated and growing since June 2020, several more young saplings grown from its acorns visible in Sept 2023 photos. The tree itself is photographed alive and standing in those Sept 2023 images, so the decline is real but the tree is not dead. This is a genuine condition change between the 2014 'Good' rating and the 2023 decline report; note both. Listed on the National Trust's Significant Tree Register as well as the City of Hobart register, so it has two independent confirmations of identity and location, though the tree's age itself rests on the unconfirmed Gallipoli story. Good writer hook: an oak grown (maybe) from a Gallipoli seed, standing at Australia's best-preserved colonial street corner, now being actively propagated because the original is fading.

name: The Dawn Redwoods of Elizabeth Street

location.address: 81 Elizabeth Street, road reserve in front of the former Commonwealth Bank building, Hobart

access: Free, public road reserve/footpath, always visible
transport: Central Hobart CBD, on Elizabeth Street near the Elizabeth/Collins Street corner
verify_notes: City of Hobart Significant Tree Register ref E7, three Dawn Redwoods (objectids 1197-1199, coordinates within about 20m of each other) registered and described AS A GROUP: 'the trees as a group of three provide a striking aesthetic in this sparsely vegetated area of the city' (Category 1) and 'a significant element in the streetscape... locally very recognisable' (Category 6). Folded these three register rows into one entry rather than three: the register itself treats them as a single significance record (one reference number, one data sheet, one reason), they stand within 20m of each other in a road reserve outside a single building, and there is one obvious place to stand to see all three, which is exactly the compact-ensemble case the collectible-point rule allows. Single-sourced: only the register record found, no independent second source located after searching; flag accordingly. No age given anywhere in the register data sheet, only the species and significance reasoning. Species itself is notable: Metasequoia was known only from fossils until living specimens were found in China in 1941, so any planting here postdates that rediscovery. Good writer hook: a species presumed extinct until 1941, planted in triplicate outside a Hobart bank.

name: The Norfolk Island Pine of Ingle Hall

location.address: 89-93 Macquarie Street, outside Ingle Hall at the corner of Macquarie and Argyle Streets, Hobart

access: Free, public street corner, always visible
transport: Central Hobart CBD, corner of Macquarie and Argyle Streets
verify_notes: City of Hobart Significant Tree Register ref M13: Category 1 (outstanding aesthetic significance), 'visually very striking, and stands out even amongst tall buildings... interesting co-dominant trunk form', plus Category 6 local significance. Second source: Hello Hobart (Feb 2025) quotes Greg Karin, owner of New Town Station Nursery, naming it his favourite tree in the city: 'It never changes much, it's slow-growing with a striking vertical form' and that it 'has witnessed plenty of change in Hobart over the years'. Stands outside Ingle Hall, a Georgian-era heritage building (part of the University of Tasmania's Conservatorium of Music), at what the same article calls one of Hobart's most significant urban trees. No documented planting date or age. Good writer hook: a slow-growing sentinel with a forked, co-dominant trunk outside one of Hobart's oldest Georgian buildings, picked out by a local arborist as his favourite tree in the city.

name: The Bhutan Cypress of Brisbane Street
transport: Central Hobart CBD, on Brisbane Street
verify_notes: City of Hobart Significant Tree Register ref B25: Category 6 local significance only, 'a very strong component of the streetscape, particularly given its vertical, conical form, and its loss would be detrimental to the community'. Single-sourced: no independent second source found after searching for this specific tree; flag accordingly. No age or dimension data in the register sheet. Bhutan cypress is uncommon as a street tree in Australia (native to the Himalayan foothills), which is itself the interesting fact rather than age or size. Genuinely the thinnest of this batch: ships because it clears the register + streetscape-significance bar, but a writer should not oversell it.

name: The Douglas Fir of the Botanical Gardens

location.address: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, 11 Lower Domain Road, Hobart

access: Free, public botanical garden, open daily 8am-5pm (Apr-Sep) or 8am-6.30pm (Oct-Mar), gold-coin donation encouraged, no compulsory entry fee
transport: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, Queens Domain, short drive or bus from Hobart CBD; free parking near the gates
verify_notes: City of Hobart Significant Tree Register ref L24 (data sheet photo credited Dr A MacFadyen, RTBG, 2006): Category 2, outstanding dimensions. National Trust (trusttrees.org.au) independently confirms: planted/germinated 1 Jan 1894 (nominal date), 30m tall, 1m diameter, condition 'Excellent' as measured 26 March 2014, part of the Gardens' 'important plant collections' with social and historic value. Age given here (128-134) is calculated forward from the 1894 planting date to 2026; the National Trust page's own displayed 'age' figure is stale relative to its 2014 measurement date, so the range is derived rather than copied verbatim. RTBG was founded in 1818, the second-oldest botanical garden in Australia, and its Pinetum/conifer collection (this tree's setting) dates mostly to the 19th century and is described by the Gardens themselves as one of the most significant conifer collections in the Southern Hemisphere. Good writer hook: a tree older than Federation, thriving in a collection the Gardens themselves call one of the finest of its kind south of the equator.

name: The Queensland Kauri of the Botanical Gardens

location.address: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, 11 Lower Domain Road, Hobart

access: Free, public botanical garden, open daily 8am-5pm (Apr-Sep) or 8am-6.30pm (Oct-Mar), gold-coin donation encouraged, no compulsory entry fee
transport: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, Queens Domain, short drive or bus from Hobart CBD; free parking near the gates
verify_notes: City of Hobart Significant Tree Register ref L18 (photo credited Dr A MacFadyen, RTBG, 2006): all four of Category 1 (aesthetic), Category 2 (outstanding dimensions), Category 3 (very old or venerable) and Category 8 (rare or of very localised distribution). This is the most heavily-qualified register entry found in this pass. National Trust confirms independently: 39m tall, 1m diameter, condition 'Excellent' as measured 28 March 2014, first classified 20 Dec 1994 (so it has been on record for over 30 years). No documented age from either source (National Trust lists it as '?'); leave age fields empty rather than guess, per the missing-age rule. Species native to Queensland rainforest and coastal areas, well outside its natural range this far south, which is presumably why the register flags it as rare/localised in a Tasmanian context. Good writer hook: a 39-metre subtropical rainforest giant, growing further south of its natural range than almost any other Kauri in the country.

name: The Giant Sequoias of the Botanical Gardens

location.address: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, entrance drive, 11 Lower Domain Road, Hobart

access: Free, public botanical garden, open daily 8am-5pm (Apr-Sep) or 8am-6.30pm (Oct-Mar), gold-coin donation encouraged, no compulsory entry fee
transport: Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, Queens Domain, short drive or bus from Hobart CBD; free parking near the gates
verify_notes: City of Hobart Significant Tree Register ref L4 ('Big Tree (Wellingtonia)', an old common name for the species; photo credited Dr A MacFadyen, RTBG, 2006): Category 2 (outstanding dimensions) and Category 3 (very old or venerable). National Trust independently confirms and describes this record as documenting 'a pair of Giant Sequoias positioned at the entrance drive' of the Gardens, classified as significant on 21 Apr 1997, germination date given as 1 Jan 1879, 36m tall, 2m diameter, condition 'Excellent' as measured 27 March 2014. Treating this as one entry for a pair standing together at the Gardens' entrance drive, the same reasoning as the Elizabeth Street redwoods: one register record, one obvious place to stand, a compact famous pair rather than a scattered planting. Do not confuse with the different, larger Giant Sequoia noted separately in this register at 7 Lower Domain Road (Government House grounds, objectid 1331): that one is a single, different tree on restricted land and is recorded separately in leads/blocked. Age here (145-149) is calculated forward from the 1879 germination date to 2026. Good writer hook: two California giants, planted the same year, still marking the entrance drive of Australia's second-oldest botanical garden nearly 150 years later.
